claim: Arabidopsis thaliana roots show coordinated growth involving local interactions between adjacent non-mobile cells to sustain the optimal exploration of soil-derived resources.
source: For example, Arabidopsis thaliana roots show coordinated growth involving local interactions between adjacent non-mobile cells to sustain the optimal exploration of soil-derived resources (O'Brien et al., 2016), and to provide water and mineral absorption as well as stability on the ground (Chapman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (O'Brien et al., 2016).

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana roots provide water and mineral absorption as well as stability on the ground.
source: For example, Arabidopsis thaliana roots show coordinated growth involving local interactions between adjacent non-mobile cells to sustain the optimal exploration of soil-derived resources (O'Brien et al., 2016), and to provide water and mineral absorption as well as stability on the ground (Chapman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chapman et al., 2012).

claim: The root elongates along the principal direction of growth during the late stages of embryogenesis.
source: The root elongates along the principal direction of growth (referred to as the anisotropy) during the late stages of embryogenesis but the mechanisms underlying the emergence of root growth anisotropy are poorly understood (Bou Daher et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Bou Daher et al., 2018).

claim: The mechanisms underlying the emergence of root growth anisotropy are poorly understood.
source: The root elongates along the principal direction of growth (referred to as the anisotropy) during the late stages of embryogenesis but the mechanisms underlying the emergence of root growth anisotropy are poorly understood (Bou Daher et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Bou Daher et al., 2018).

claim: Root maturation follows a sequence of asymmetric cell divisions and cell expansion that involves the growth regulator auxin.
source: Root maturates following a sequence of asymmetric cell divisions and cell expansion that involves the growth regulator auxin (Adamowski and Friml, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Adamowski and Friml, 2015).

claim: Auxin is transported in a directional (polar) manner.
source: Auxin is transported in a directional (polar) manner (Wisniewska et al., 2006) that requires the polar subcellular localization of the PIN-FORMED (PIN) auxin efflux carriers (Adamowski and Friml, 2015; Benková et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Wisniewska et al., 2006).

claim: Polar auxin transport requires the polar subcellular localization of the PIN-FORMED (PIN) auxin efflux carriers.
source: Auxin is transported in a directional (polar) manner (Wisniewska et al., 2006) that requires the polar subcellular localization of the PIN-FORMED (PIN) auxin efflux carriers (Adamowski and Friml, 2015; Benková et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adamowski and Friml, 2015; Benková et al., 2003).

claim: Auxin controls cell elongation through weakening or stiffening of the cell walls depending on threshold concentrations.
source: Subsequently, auxin controls cell elongation through weakening or stiffening of the cell walls depending on threshold concentrations (Barbez et al., 2017; Majda and Robert, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Barbez et al., 2017; Majda and Robert, 2018).

claim: Cell growth is associated with changes in cytoskeleton components, such as cortical microtubules (CMTs), actin, and cell wall elements.
source: In general, cell growth is associated with changes in cytoskeleton components, such as cortical microtubules (CMTs), actin, and cell wall elements (Adamowski et al., 2019; Siegrist and Doe, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adamowski et al., 2019; Siegrist and Doe, 2007).

claim: CMTs integrate mechanical stresses into dynamic cytoskeleton rearrangements.
source: Among those, CMTs integrate mechanical stresses (Hamant et al., 2019; Hamant and Haswell, 2017) into dynamic cytoskeleton rearrangements, constraining the directional trafficking of membrane proteins, small signaling molecules, and cell wall building components (Adamowski et al., 2019; Siegrist and Doe, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hamant et al., 2019; Hamant and Haswell, 2017).

claim: CMTs constrain the directional trafficking of membrane proteins, small signaling molecules, and cell wall building components.
source: Among those, CMTs integrate mechanical stresses (Hamant et al., 2019; Hamant and Haswell, 2017) into dynamic cytoskeleton rearrangements, constraining the directional trafficking of membrane proteins, small signaling molecules, and cell wall building components (Adamowski et al., 2019; Siegrist and Doe, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adamowski et al., 2019; Siegrist and Doe, 2007).

claim: Several computational models of root development yielded important insights into auxin-dependent growth and zonation of mature roots.
source: In the last decade, several computational models of root development yielded important insights into auxin-dependent growth and zonation of mature roots (Morales-Tapia and Cruz-Ramírez, 2016; Rutten and Ten Tusscher, 2019; Wabnik et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Morales-Tapia and Cruz-Ramírez, 2016; Rutten and Ten Tusscher, 2019; Wabnik et al., 2011).

claim: Previous root development models typically incorporate pre-defined patterns of polar auxin flow on idealized geometries.
source: Yet, these models typically incorporate pre-defined patterns of polar auxin flow on idealized geometries (e.g. cell grids)(Band et al., 2014; Grieneisen et al., 2007; Mähönen et al., 2014; Mironova et al., 2010; Wabnik et al., 2013) and rarely integrate growth mechanics (De Vos et al., 2014; Fozard et al., 2013; Jensen and Fozard, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Band et al., 2014; Grieneisen et al., 2007; Mähönen et al., 2014; Mironova et al., 2010; Wabnik et al., 2013).

claim: Previous root development models rarely integrate growth mechanics.
source: Yet, these models typically incorporate pre-defined patterns of polar auxin flow on idealized geometries (e.g. cell grids)(Band et al., 2014; Grieneisen et al., 2007; Mähönen et al., 2014; Mironova et al., 2010; Wabnik et al., 2013) and rarely integrate growth mechanics (De Vos et al., 2014; Fozard et al., 2013; Jensen and Fozard, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (De Vos et al., 2014; Fozard et al., 2013; Jensen and Fozard, 2015).

claim: Plant embryogenesis follows the fertilization of the egg, and successive formation of the zygote.
source: Plant embryogenesis follows the fertilization of the egg, and successive formation of the zygote (Park and Harada, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Park and Harada, 2008).

claim: The zygote contracts transiently to later elongate, setting the embryonic axis within a few hours.
source: Initially, the zygote contracts transiently to later elongate, setting the embryonic axis within a few hours; after several cell divisions, the aerial and root parts are already clearly distinguishable (Kimata et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kimata et al., 2016).

claim: After several cell divisions, the aerial and root parts are already clearly distinguishable.
source: Initially, the zygote contracts transiently to later elongate, setting the embryonic axis within a few hours; after several cell divisions, the aerial and root parts are already clearly distinguishable (Kimata et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kimata et al., 2016).

claim: The stem cell niche is initiated during the 'heart' developmental stage.
source: The stem cell niche is initiated during the 'heart' developmental stage (ten Hove et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (ten Hove et al., 2015).

claim: The heart-stage of A. thaliana embryo provides an ideal starting point for the entire organ establishment.
source: Therefore, we chose this stage for the construction of the computer model of the root meristem as it provides an ideal starting point for the entire organ establishment, assuming uniform growth and non-polar distribution of auxin transporters and a set of differentiated cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about model construction.

claim: 2D cellular meshes were built by digitizing confocal microscopy images of the heart-stage of A. thaliana embryo using MorphoGraphX.
source: By digitizing the confocal microscopy images of the heart-stage of A. thaliana embryo, we build 2D cellular meshes with MorphoGraphX (Barbier de Reuille et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the MorphoGraphX software (Barbier de Reuille et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organ growth framework is based on Position-based Dynamics (PBD), a modeling technique adapted from computer graphics.
source: To model the pure growth mechanics at a single-cell resolution, we used these meshes at the start of each simulation. We implemented the organ growth framework based on Position-based Dynamics (PBD), a modeling technique adapted from computer graphics (Müller et al., 2007; Marconi and Wabnik, 2021a; Marconi and Wabnik, 2021b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Müller et al., 2007; Marconi and Wabnik, 2021a; Marconi and Wabnik, 2021b) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PBD approximates physical forces using a set of growth constraints.
source: PBD approximates physical forces using a set of growth constraints (Müller et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Müller et al., 2007).

claim: PBD constraints reproduce internal turgor pressure, viscoelastic behavior of plant cell walls, and mechanical deformation (strain).
source: These constraints reproduce internal turgor pressure, viscoelastic behavior of plant cell walls, and mechanical deformation (strain) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; see Materials and methods section for PBD details).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and the Materials and methods section.

claim: PBD avoids the slow numerical time integration step used in classical force-based methods.
source: Because these constraints are sequentially projected over the vertices of the 2D meshes by directly updating the position of vertices, the PBD method avoids the slow numerical time integration step used in classical force-based methods (Müller et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Müller et al., 2007).

claim: PBD is faster and more stable than other physically based approaches such as mass-spring systems or finite element methods (FEM).
source: Thus PBD is faster and more stable than other physically based approaches such as mass-spring systems (Müller et al., 2007) or finite element methods (FEM)(Bidhendi and Geitmann, 2018; Fayant et al., 2010), and therefore ideally suited for complex organ modeling at cellular resolutions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Müller et al., 2007; Bidhendi and Geitmann, 2018; Fayant et al., 2010).

claim: The numerical stability of PBD is critical when dealing with growing entities and expanding complexities.
source: This numerical stability of PBD is critical when dealing with growing entities and expanding complexities.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the advantages of PBD.

claim: PBD can be explicitly defined on a single-cell or even subcellular level which remains a major challenge for continuous mechanics FEM-based approaches.
source: Another important advantage of using PBD is that this method can be explicitly defined on a single-cell or even subcellular level which remains a major challenge for continuous mechanics FEM-based approaches (Boudon et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Boudon et al., 2015).

claim: Differential cell growth produced by mechanical interactions may regulate organogenesis independently from genetic control.
source: Recent studies suggest that differential cell growth produced by mechanical interactions may regulate organogenesis independently from genetic control, and potentially feedback on it.
evidence: The claim is based on recent studies mentioned in the text.

claim: Arabidopsis trichomes emerge from sepals through differential cell growth.
source: Some examples include Arabidopsis trichomes emerging from sepals (Hervieux et al., 2017) or the tomato shoot apical meristem (Kierzkowski et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Hervieux et al., 2017).

claim: In the hypocotyl, the CMT array is transversely oriented to the hypocotyl growth axis during the elongation phase.
source: Interestingly, in the hypocotyl, the CMT array is transversely oriented to the hypocotyl growth axis during the elongation phase and longitudinally oriented when elongation stops (Le et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Le et al., 2005).

claim: In the hypocotyl, the CMT array is longitudinally oriented when elongation stops.
source: Interestingly, in the hypocotyl, the CMT array is transversely oriented to the hypocotyl growth axis during the elongation phase and longitudinally oriented when elongation stops (Le et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Le et al., 2005).

claim: We lack a mechanistic understanding of how CMTs, actin, and cell wall components together regulate anisotropy.
source: Despite these observations, we still lack a mechanistic understanding of CMTs, actin, and cell wall component together regulate anisotropy which limits detailed modeling of individual components of the cytoskeleton network.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of current knowledge.

claim: The outcome of processes involved in cytoskeleton dynamics is approximated by an abstract 'anisotropy factor' (AF) in the model.
source: To avoid additional complexities, we decided to approximate the outcome of processes involved in cytoskeleton dynamics by an abstract 'anisotropy factor' (AF).
evidence: The claim describes a modeling decision made by the authors.

claim: In the model, the AF denotes the tendency of the cell to grow anisotropically and can be reoriented through the action of external stimuli or forces.
source: In the model, the AF denotes the tendency of the cell to grow anisotropically and can be reoriented through the action of external stimuli or forces.
evidence: The claim describes a property of the model.

claim: The AF reorientation follows cell deformation, creating a feedback mechanism that further reinforces the anisotropic growth.
source: Explicitly, the AF reorientation follows cell deformation, creating a feedback mechanism that further reinforces the anisotropic growth (see Materials and methods for more details, Position-based dynamics implementation).
evidence: The claim describes a mechanism in the model.

claim: Differential growth of tissues at the root-shoot interface (RSI) during late embryogenesis could potentially trigger initial symmetry breaking, leading to anisotropic root growth.
source: We then hypothesized that perhaps differential growth of tissues at the root-shoot interface (RSI) during late embryogenesis could potentially trigger initial symmetry breaking, leading to anisotropic root growth (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis tested by the authors, supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1A–B.

claim: Uniform growth of root and RSI results in strong isotropic growth at the basal part of the embryo (BPE).
source: To test this hypothesis, we performed model simulations first by assuming uniform growth of root and RSI (Figure 1A, Figure 1—video 1). In this scenario, we could only observe the strong isotropic growth at the basal part of the embryo (BPE) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Faster growth of the BPE compared to the adjacent embryonic tissues yields a strong anisotropic expansion.
source: In contrast, faster growth of the BPE compared to the adjacent embryonic tissues yields a strong anisotropic expansion (Figure 1B and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: A slowly growing RSI prevents the expansion of the faster-growing BPE in the radial direction.
source: The plausible explanation for this is that a slowly growing RSI prevents the expansion of the faster-growing BPE in the radial direction; the BPE gradually enlarges longitudinally, generating deformation (strain).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: The BPE gradually enlarges longitudinally, generating deformation (strain).
source: The plausible explanation for this is that a slowly growing RSI prevents the expansion of the faster-growing BPE in the radial direction; the BPE gradually enlarges longitudinally, generating deformation (strain).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: Deformation feeds back on the BPE growth, creating the desired anisotropy.
source: Then, this deformation feeds back on the BPE growth, creating the desired anisotropy.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: The emerging root radicle grew ~4 x faster than the adjacent hypocotyl in the initial outgrowth phase.
source: We tested these model predictions by quantifying the growth increase over 6 hr in radicle and hypocotyl of young seedlings using time-lapse confocal microscopy imaging (Figure 1C; Zhu et al., 2019). Indeed, the emerging root radicle grew ~4 x faster than the adjacent hypocotyl (Figure 1D) in the initial outgrowth phase which further supports our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1D, with a citation to the imaging method (Zhu et al., 2019).

claim: Anisotropy forms gradually without predominant growth conflicts, but is rather dictated by differential growth at the RSI.
source: To further confirm that growth anisotropy indeed emerges from differential growth rates, and not from an existing conflict of growth direction, we quantified the degree of cellular anisotropy in both scenarios and found that anisotropy forms gradually without predominant growth conflicts, but is rather dictated by differential growth at the RSI (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: After a short period of growth after which the anisotropy is established, the organ is still capable of maintaining anisotropic elongation even if differential growth at the RSI is abolished.
source: After a short period of growth after which the anisotropy is established, the organ is still capable of maintaining anisotropic elongation even if differential growth at the RSI is abolished (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Differential growth between adjacent tissues is, in principle, sufficient to generate root growth anisotropy.
source: This result further strengthens the notion that the differential growth between adjacent tissues is, in principle, sufficient to generate root growth anisotropy.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: Anisotropic root growth results from differential growth rates of neighboring tissues.
source: In summary, model simulations and experiments jointly suggest that anisotropic root growth results from differential growth rates of neighboring tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by both model simulations and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oriented growth restricts root elongation, primarily along the longitudinal axis.
source: This oriented growth further restricts root elongation, primarily along the longitudinal axis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: Cellular auxin levels play a key role in regulating growth in A. thaliana root.
source: In A. thaliana root, cellular auxin levels play a key role in regulating growth, and auxin levels can be tuned through intercellular transport, involving auxin influx and efflux carriers (Adamowski and Friml, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Adamowski and Friml, 2015).

claim: Auxin levels can be tuned through intercellular transport, involving auxin influx and efflux carriers.
source: In A. thaliana root, cellular auxin levels play a key role in regulating growth, and auxin levels can be tuned through intercellular transport, involving auxin influx and efflux carriers (Adamowski and Friml, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Adamowski and Friml, 2015).

claim: Auxin influx carriers of the AUX/LAX family are typically uniformly distributed around the cell membranes.
source: While auxin influx carriers of the AUX/LAX family are typically uniformly distributed around the cell membranes (Kleine-Vehn and Friml, 2008), PIN auxin efflux carriers show polar subcellular localization in the root that directs the auxin flow rootward or shootward (Wisniewska et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kleine-Vehn and Friml, 2008).

claim: PIN auxin efflux carriers show polar subcellular localization in the root that directs the auxin flow rootward or shootward.
source: While auxin influx carriers of the AUX/LAX family are typically uniformly distributed around the cell membranes (Kleine-Vehn and Friml, 2008), PIN auxin efflux carriers show polar subcellular localization in the root that directs the auxin flow rootward or shootward (Wisniewska et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Wisniewska et al., 2006).

claim: PIN proteins are prominent markers of cell polarity that continuously recycle between the plasma membrane and endosomal compartments.
source: Also, PIN proteins are prominent markers of cell polarity that continuously recycle between the plasma membrane and endosomal compartments (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2011).

claim: Chemical treatments of actin, microtubules, and cell wall components with disruptive agents suggest the involvement of these cytoskeleton components in the regulation of PIN polar trafficking.
source: The mechanisms underlying PIN trafficking are still poorly understood, however, chemical treatments of actin, microtubules, and cell wall components with disruptive agents suggest the involvement of these cytoskeleton components in the regulation of PIN polar trafficking (Baskin, 2005; Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008; Feraru et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Baskin, 2005; Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008; Feraru et al., 2011).

claim: The coexistence of growth polarity and dominant PIN localization in many root cells suggests that growth anisotropy and PIN polarity may be mechanistically entangled.
source: The coexistence of growth polarity and dominant PIN localization in many roots cells suggests that growth anisotropy and PIN polarity may be mechanistically entangled as previously shown for the shoot apical meristem (Heisler et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Heisler et al., 2010).

claim: Tissue mechanics control growth anisotropy.
source: Because tissue mechanics control growth anisotropy it is plausible to conceive possible feedback on PIN polarity that modulates deposition of the cell wall and cytoskeleton components (Braybrook and Peaucelle, 2013; Feraru et al., 2011; Heisler et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Braybrook and Peaucelle, 2013; Feraru et al., 2011; Heisler et al., 2010).

claim: It is plausible to conceive possible feedback on PIN polarity that modulates deposition of the cell wall and cytoskeleton components.
source: Because tissue mechanics control growth anisotropy it is plausible to conceive possible feedback on PIN polarity that modulates deposition of the cell wall and cytoskeleton components (Braybrook and Peaucelle, 2013; Feraru et al., 2011; Heisler et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Braybrook and Peaucelle, 2013; Feraru et al., 2011; Heisler et al., 2010).

claim: The AF restricts the axis along which PINs are delivered.
source: Based on these experimental observations, we thought of a scenario where the AF restricts the axis along which PINs are delivered.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on experimental observations.

claim: The AF restricts the axis along which PINs are delivered, which recreates the correlation between anisotropic growth and PIN localization, but does not determine the preferential direction (rootward, shootward, or lateral) of auxin flow.
source: This would recreate the correlation between anisotropic growth and PIN localization, but it would not determine the preferential direction (rootward, shootward, or lateral) of auxin flow.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the proposed scenario.

claim: To define the actual direction of auxin movement in the model, other mechanisms of likely biochemical nature are required.
source: Therefore, to define the actual direction of auxin movement in our model other mechanisms of likely biochemical nature are required.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model design.

claim: Auxin modulates the trafficking of PIN proteins in a feedback-dependent manner by a yet unknown molecular mechanism.
source: Auxin modulates the trafficking of PIN proteins in a feedback-dependent manner by a yet unknown molecular mechanism (Adamowski and Friml, 2015; Narasimhan et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adamowski and Friml, 2015; Narasimhan et al., 2021).

claim: Several theories for the establishment of PIN polarities have been proposed, including sensing the net auxin flux through the cell.
source: Several theories for the establishment of PIN polarities have been proposed, i.e. through sensing the net auxin flux through the cell (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008), auxin concentrations (Jönsson et al., 2006; Merks et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2006; Wabnik et al., 2010), the auxin gradient inside the cell (Kramer, 2009) or their combination (Cieslak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008).

claim: Several theories for the establishment of PIN polarities have been proposed, including sensing auxin concentrations.
source: Several theories for the establishment of PIN polarities have been proposed, i.e. through sensing the net auxin flux through the cell (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008), auxin concentrations (Jönsson et al., 2006; Merks et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2006; Wabnik et al., 2010), the auxin gradient inside the cell (Kramer, 2009) or their combination (Cieslak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Jönsson et al., 2006; Merks et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2006; Wabnik et al., 2010).

claim: Several theories for the establishment of PIN polarities have been proposed, including sensing the auxin gradient inside the cell.
source: Several theories for the establishment of PIN polarities have been proposed, i.e. through sensing the net auxin flux through the cell (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008), auxin concentrations (Jönsson et al., 2006; Merks et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2006; Wabnik et al., 2010), the auxin gradient inside the cell (Kramer, 2009) or their combination (Cieslak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kramer, 2009).

claim: Two scenarios of the auxin effect on its PIN-mediated transport were tested and integrated into the mechanical growth model.
source: We tested scenarios of the auxin effect on its PIN-mediated transport using two scenarios that were integrated into the mechanical growth model (Figure 1) and are compatible with recent experimental observations (Narasimhan et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations and a citation to recent experimental observations (Narasimhan et al., 2021).

claim: In the 'with-the-flux model', cells sense auxin flux through the membrane and adjust PIN allocation to the plasma membrane in a positive feedback-dependent manner.
source: In the first scenario, cells would sense auxin flux through the membrane (also called 'with-the-flux model')(Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008) and adjust PIN allocation to the plasma membrane in a positive feedback-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The exact molecular mechanism behind auxin flux sensing is to be demonstrated and it may involve membrane-associated protein kinases.
source: Despite that, the exact molecular mechanism behind auxin flux sensing is to be demonstrated and it may involve membrane-associated protein kinases (Hajný et al., 2020; Marhava et al., 2018; Michniewicz et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hajný et al., 2020; Marhava et al., 2018; Michniewicz et al., 2007).

claim: The 'regulator-polarizer' model implements a potential mechanism behind auxin flux sensing.
source: Therefore, we explored a second scenario for PIN polarization that we named 'regulator-polarizer' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D). The regulator-polarizer model implements a potential mechanism behind auxin flux sensing (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Feugier and Iwasa, 2006; Mitchison, 1997; Rolland-Lagan and Prusinkiewicz, 2005; Stoma et al., 2008) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In the 'regulator-polarizer' model, a putative regulator detects auxin passing through a plasma membrane, becomes activated and freely diffuses in the plasma membrane.
source: Briefly, a putative regulator (i.e. a general phosphatase [Michniewicz et al., 2007]) detects auxin passing through a plasma membrane, it becomes activated and freely diffuses in the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Michniewicz et al., 2007).

claim: In the 'regulator-polarizer' model, the regulator inhibits a polarizer that in turn activates PINs.
source: This regulator inhibits a polarizer (e.g. a dedicated protein kinase that phosphorylates PIN Hajný et al., 2020; Michniewicz et al., 2007) that in turn activates PINs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hajný et al., 2020; Michniewicz et al., 2007).

claim: At the side where the concentration of regulator is high enough to overcome the polarizer, no PINs are recruited.
source: Therefore, at the side where the concentration of regulator is high enough to overcome the polarizer, no PINs are recruited.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the 'regulator-polarizer' model mechanism.

claim: The model combines exo- or endocytosis and lateral diffusion of PIN proteins into one general trafficking term.
source: Our model combines exo- or endocytosis and lateral diffusion of PIN proteins into one general trafficking term, which is a crude simplification required to reduce model complexities (see Materials and methods for more details, Auxin transport module description).
evidence: The claim describes a simplification made in the model.

claim: PIN recruitment parameters were fitted to the experimentally derived kinetics of PIN trafficking after cell division.
source: However, to incorporate quantitative data in the model, PIN recruitment parameters were fitted to the experimentally derived kinetics of PIN trafficking after cell division (Figure 2K; Glanc et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2K and a citation to published research (Glanc et al., 2018).

claim: The model does not distinguish between different PIN families.
source: Currently, we do not distinguish in our model between different PIN families (Sauer and Kleine-Vehn, 2019), instead, all PINs are distributed according to one of the two PIN polarization scenarios (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes a simplification made in the model, with a citation to published research (Sauer and Kleine-Vehn, 2019).

claim: PINs in the columella are distributed uniformly among membrane sections, to reproduce the observed PIN3 distribution.
source: The only exception to this general rule is that PINs in the columella are distributed uniformly among membrane sections, to reproduce the observed PIN3 distribution (Friml et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Friml et al., 2002).

claim: Columella cells redistribute PINs over the totality of the membrane and not to a specific polar section, causing lower overall PINs levels when compared to experimental observations.
source: Given that maximal PINs abundance threshold is the same for all cell types, the fact that columella cells redistribute PINs over the totality of the membrane and not to a specific polar section causes lower overall PINs levels when compared to experimental observations (Blilou et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model design, with a citation to experimental observations (Blilou et al., 2005).

claim: The model assumes uniform distribution of AUX/LAX carriers in all cell types.
source: Other assumptions of our model are the uniform distribution of AUX/LAX carriers (Swarup et al., 2001) in all cell types, and the omission of other transporters such as ABCB transporters (Cho and Cho, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Swarup et al., 2001).

claim: The model omits other transporters such as ABCB transporters.
source: Other assumptions of our model are the uniform distribution of AUX/LAX carriers (Swarup et al., 2001) in all cell types, and the omission of other transporters such as ABCB transporters (Cho and Cho, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Cho and Cho, 2013).

claim: The combined mechano-biochemical model was able to reproduce a complex PIN polarization network from an initially non-polar scenario.
source: Our combined mechano-biochemical model was able to reproduce a complex PIN polarization network from an initially non-polar scenario (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 5E-G and Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 5E-G and Figure 2—videos 1 and 2.

claim: The dynamic PIN polarization network includes rootward PIN localization in vascular tissues and shootward localization in the outermost epidermis that closely follow experimentally observed patterns.
source: This dynamic network includes rootward PIN localization in vascular tissues and shootward localization in the outermost epidermis that closely follow experimentally observed patterns (see Figure 1 in Blilou et al., 2005 and Figure 2 in Tanaka et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Blilou et al., 2005; Tanaka et al., 2006).

claim: PIN polarity patterns emerge from mechanical constraints, auxin flow, and auxin-mediated growth.
source: The model predicts that PIN polarity patterns emerge from mechanical constraints, auxin flow, and auxin-mediated growth – likely the elements of the same feedback mechanism.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: The absence of mechanical constraints regulating PIN localization results in incorrect auxin/PIN distribution, with the disappearance of the auxin maximum and a general lack of PIN polarity.
source: For both the 'auxin flux (Figure 2—figure supplement 7A, B) and the 'regulator-polarizer' (Figure 2—figure supplement 7C, D) scenarios, the absence of mechanical constraints regulating PIN localization results in incorrect auxin/PIN distribution, with the disappearance of the auxin maximum and a general lack of PIN polarity.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7A, B, C, D.

claim: Mechanical deformation is strongly involved in the root cell polarity patterning mechanisms.
source: This important finding suggests a strong involvement of mechanical deformation in the root cell polarity patterning mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: The model predicts bidirectional (shootward and rootward) 'bipolar' localization of PIN proteins in the cortex tissues in the transition region that is marked by the termination of lateral root cap (LRC).
source: Another intriguing emergent property of the model was the bidirectional (shootward and rootward) 'bipolar' localization of PIN proteins in the cortex tissues (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5F) in the transition region that is marked by the termination of lateral root cap (LRC).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5F.

claim: The 'bipolar' PIN localization in the cortex has been previously observed in experiments close to the transition zone.
source: This 'bipolar' PIN localization in the cortex has been previously observed in experiments close to the transition zone (Ötvös et al., 2021; Sauer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ötvös et al., 2021; Sauer et al., 2006).

claim: Model simulations suggest that the bipolar cortex PIN localization is likely the result of the conflict between the shootward auxin flow from LRC/epidermis and the rootward auxin flow in the vascular tissues.
source: Yet, the function of this phenomenon remains largely unknown. Model simulations suggest that the bipolar cortex PIN localization is likely the result of the conflict between the shootward auxin flow from LRC/epidermis and the rootward auxin flow in the vascular tissues (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5F).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5F.

claim: There is a subtle difference between the 'auxin-flux' and the 'regulator-polarizer' scenarios regarding the PIN lateralization pattern.
source: However, we observed a subtle difference between the 'auxin-flux' (Figure 2F) and the 'regulator-polarizer' (Figure 2—figure supplement 5F) scenarios regarding the PIN lateralization pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5F.

claim: The 'auxin-flux' scenario allocates PINs based on global flux patterns whereas the 'regulator-polarizer' scenario depends on local auxin concentrations at a given membrane segment.
source: The likely explanation for these small differences is that the 'auxin-flux' scenario allocates PINs based on global flux patterns whereas the 'regulator-polarizer' scenario depends on local auxin concentrations at a given membrane segment.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model design.

claim: Computer simulations indicate a plausible mechano-biochemical model that accounts for auxin-dependent anisotropic root growth and PIN polarity establishment.
source: Taken together, computer simulations indicate a plausible mechano-biochemical model that accounts for auxin-dependent anisotropic root growth and PIN polarity establishment.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the model simulation results.

claim: Model simulations reconstitute the complex PIN polarity network in the simulated root growth, suggesting the presence of lateral auxin transport from the external tissues (epidermis and LRC) into the cortex and the stele.
source: Our model simulations reconstitute the complex PIN polarity network in the simulated root growth (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 5F-G), suggesting the presence of lateral auxin transport from the external tissues (epidermis and LRC) into the cortex and the stele (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 5F-G, Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 5E.

claim: The 'bipolar' PIN localization could drive polar auxin redistribution towards inner tissues, consistent with the phenomenon described as the reflux loop.
source: This 'bipolar' PIN localization (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5F) could drive polar auxin redistribution towards inner tissues, that is consistent with the phenomenon described as the reflux loop (Benková et al., 2003; Grieneisen et al., 2007; Paponov et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5F and citations to published research (Benková et al., 2003; Grieneisen et al., 2007; Paponov et al., 2005).

claim: Lateral auxin transport between the epidermis and cortex might be further enhanced by plasmodesmata-dependent diffusion.
source: Although not covered by our model, this lateral auxin transport between the epidermis and cortex might be further enhanced by plasmodesmata-dependent diffusion (Mellor et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Mellor et al., 2020).

claim: It is the directionality of transport mediated by PINs that is critical for the growth coordination of adjacent epidermis and cortex tissues.
source: Yet, it is a directionality of transport mediated by PINs that is critical for the growth coordination of adjacent epidermis and cortex tissues (Ötvös et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Ötvös et al., 2021).

claim: Artificially preventing lateral auxin transport results in a negligible amount of auxin entering the cortex, with no lateral auxin influx originated from the epidermis.
source: To further investigate the importance of a dynamic PIN localization network for the sustained growth of the root, we performed model simulations by artificially preventing lateral auxin transport (Figure 3A and B). We found that a negligible amount of auxin enters the cortex, but no lateral auxin influx originated from the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The bipolar PIN localization is absent in 'no-reflux' simulations.
source: Additionally, the bipolar PIN localization was absent in these 'no-reflux' simulations (Figure 3C and Figure 3—video 1) compared to the reference model (Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3C, Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1.

claim: PIN-mediated lateral transport is important for auxin redistribution in inner root tissues.
source: This finding confirms the importance of PIN-mediated lateral transport for auxin redistribution in inner root tissues.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: The lack of auxin recycling in the meristem does not seem to significantly reduce root growth rates as long as auxin is supplied from the shoot.
source: However, the lack of auxin recycling in the meristem does not seem to significantly reduce root growth rates as long as auxin is supplied from the shoot (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the simulation where there was neither reflux nor bipolar PIN localization, root growth could not be sustained over a prolonged time and the auxin inside the root eventually disappeared.
source: Therefore, to investigate the role of shoot-derived auxin source in the root growth, we artificially separated the root from the rest of the plant by removing the shoot-derived auxin source (Figure 3A–B, bottom panel). In this simulation where there was neither reflux nor bipolar PIN localization, root growth could not be sustained over a prolonged time and the auxin inside the root eventually disappeared (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3A–B, bottom panel and Figure 3E.

claim: The reflux scenario allows for the maintenance of auxin levels over a prolonged period even without the shoot-derived auxin source being removed.
source: On contrary, the reflux scenario allows for the maintenance of auxin levels over a prolonged period even without the shoot-derived auxin source being removed.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: Root growth can be further strengthened by incorporating auxin biosynthesis in the QC cells, which in theory could sustain root growth almost indefinitely.
source: Root growth can be further strengthened by incorporating auxin biosynthesis in the QC cells (Stepanova et al., 2008), which in theory could sustain root growth almost indefinitely (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3E–F and a citation to published research (Stepanova et al., 2008).

claim: The presence of an auxin reflux loop mediated by bidirectional PIN transport and diffusion in the cortex/epidermis is capable to sustain root growth for prolonged periods.
source: These results together indicate that the presence of an auxin reflux loop mediated by bidirectional PIN transport and diffusion in the cortex/epidermis is capable to sustain root growth for prolonged periods.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: Model simulations show the sequential inhibition and reinstatement of root growth after cyclic auxin removal.
source: To test how alterations in auxin levels alone would impact root growth dynamics, we successively simulated a series of external auxin applications for 6 hr by increasing the overall auxin content of the root (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—video 1). Model simulations show the sequential inhibition and reinstatement of root growth after cyclic auxin removal (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 4A–B, Figure 4C and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: Model predictions replicate the experimentally observed temporal inhibition of root growth by external auxin applications.
source: Notably, these model predictions replicate the experimentally observed temporal inhibition of root growth by external auxin applications (see Figure 1f in Fendrych et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Fendrych et al., 2018).

claim: The model can correctly recapitulate experimentally observed modulation of root growth response to externally applied auxin.
source: Our analysis indicates that our root model can correctly recapitulate experimentally observed modulation of root growth response to externally applied auxin.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the model simulation results.

claim: The balance in auxin content maintained by the network of PIN polarity is critical for the sustained growth of the root meristem.
source: Also, our model suggests that the balance in auxin content maintained by the network of PIN polarity is critical for the sustained growth of the root meristem.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: The mechano-biochemical framework for root meristem growth could be potentially used to test dynamic perturbations of root growth, such as genetic alterations and mechanical manipulations.
source: Our analysis indicates that the mechano-biochemical framework for root meristem growth could be potentially used to test dynamic perturbations of root growth, such as genetic alterations and mechanical manipulations, guiding the further design of wet-lab experiments.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applications of the model.

claim: PIN2 is an important auxin efflux carrier expressed in the most external root tissues: cortex, epidermis, and lateral root cap.
source: PIN2 is an important auxin efflux carrier expressed in the most external root tissues: cortex, epidermis, and lateral root cap (Adamowski and Friml, 2015), and steers root gravitropic responses (Rahman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adamowski and Friml, 2015; Rahman et al., 2010).

claim: PIN2 steers root gravitropic responses.
source: PIN2 is an important auxin efflux carrier expressed in the most external root tissues: cortex, epidermis, and lateral root cap (Adamowski and Friml, 2015), and steers root gravitropic responses (Rahman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Rahman et al., 2010).

claim: PIN2 loss-of-function results in defective gravitropic response largely because of disrupted auxin transport dynamics.
source: PIN2 loss-of-function results in defective gravitropic response largely because of disrupted auxin transport dynamics (Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Dhonukshe et al., 2010).

claim: Reduced levels of PINs in the outermost tissues resulted in auxin accumulation in the lateral root cap on both sides of the root.
source: To test whether our model could predict the alterations of auxin distribution observed in pin2 mutants, we performed computer simulations by reducing PIN expression rate in the epidermis, cortex, and lateral root cap (Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—video 1). The reduced levels of PINs in these outermost tissues resulted in auxin accumulation in the lateral root cap on both sides of the root (Figure 5B), which was absent in the wild-type simulations (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: Model predictions of auxin accumulation in the lateral root cap mimic experimental observations of pin2 knockdown mutant.
source: These predictions mimic experimental observations of pin2 knockdown mutant (see Figure 2f in Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Liu et al., 2018).

claim: Reduced expression of PIN-dependent transport in the inner vascular tissues predicts the alteration of auxin distribution and growth defects.
source: Similarly, the reduced expression of PIN-dependent transport in the inner vascular tissues in our model predicts the alteration of auxin distribution and growth defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—video 2.

claim: Severely reducing auxin cellular influx (by 90 % reduction of AUX/LAX expression) led to lower auxin content, reduced sensitivity to auxin, and thereby slow root growth.
source: Finally, we tested how a general knockdown of auxin cellular influx would impact root growth. Severely reducing auxin cellular influx (by 90 % reduction of AUX/LAX expression) led to lower auxin content, reduced sensitivity to auxin, and thereby slow root growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—video 3) as previously suggested (Inoue et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—video 3, and citations to published research (Inoue et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

claim: The QC is a small group of cells (four to seven in the A. thaliana root) located in the middle of the root apical meristem.
source: The QC is a small group of cells (four to seven in the A. thaliana root) located in the middle of the root apical meristem (Doerner, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Doerner, 1998).

claim: The QC divides infrequently and grows at an extremely low rate.
source: The QC divides infrequently and grows at an extremely low rate (Nawy et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Nawy et al., 2005).

claim: The QC is known to be the source of signals that inhibits differentiation of the surrounding stem cells.
source: The QC is known to be the source of signals that inhibits differentiation of the surrounding stem cells (van den Berg et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (van den Berg et al., 1997).

claim: QC cells define the correct location of the stem cell niche but also behave as independent cells by self-renewing and replenishing initials that have been displaced from their position.
source: QC cells define the correct location of the stem cell niche but also behave as independent cells by self-renewing and replenishing initials that have been displaced from their position (Kidner et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kidner et al., 2000).

claim: QC laser ablation is not lethal for the root as a new QC and stem niche are quickly reestablished a few cells above the wound in correlation with increased auxin accumulation.
source: QC laser ablation is not lethal for the root as a new QC and stem niche are quickly reestablished a few cells above the wound in correlation with increased auxin accumulation (Sabatini et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Sabatini et al., 2003).

claim: Compared to the wild-type simulations, QC ablation results in the typical auxin accumulation in the root tip being depleted, and auxin reflux in the LRC being significantly reduced, while most of the auxin coming from the shoot tends to concentrate in the cells above the ablation.
source: We replicated the same experiment in silico by removing the two QC cells from the model during a simulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5—video 4). Compared to the wild-type simulations (Figure 5A), the typical auxin accumulation in the root tip is depleted, and auxin reflux in the LRC was significantly reduced, while most of the auxin coming from the shoot tends to concentrate in the cells above the ablation, exactly as observed in experiments (see Figure 5 in Reddy et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—video 4, Figure 5A and a citation to published research (Reddy et al., 2007).

claim: Removal of the LRC led to sharp auxin accumulation in the root tip.
source: Similarly, removal of the LRC led to sharp auxin accumulation in the root tip (Figure 5C and Figure 5—video 5), largely matching empirical data (Tsugeki and Fedoroff, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—video 5, and a citation to published research (Tsugeki and Fedoroff, 1999).

claim: A. thaliana roots can survive not only after QC ablation but even after the complete excision of the root tip, as the plant can regenerate a new root tip including a complete new root apical meristem.
source: A. thaliana roots can survive not only after QC ablation but even after the complete excision of the root tip, as the plant can regenerate a new root tip including a complete new root apical meristem (Efroni et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Efroni et al., 2016).

claim: Since the stem cell niche is lost with excision, the regeneration process relies on other pluripotent dormant cell types available in the remaining stump.
source: Since the stem cell niche is lost with excision, the regeneration process relies on other pluripotent dormant cell types available in the remaining stump (Sugimoto et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Sugimoto et al., 2010).

claim: Compared to QC ablation, the removal of the root tip displays an even more radical effect on auxin patterning dynamics.
source: We tested if we could replicate this experiment by removing the entirety of the root tip during the simulation (Figure 5D and Figure 5—video 6). Compared to QC ablation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5—video 4), the removal of the root tip displays an even more radical effect on auxin patterning dynamics (Figure 5D and Figure 5—video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5D, Figure 5—video 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5—video 4.

claim: After root tip removal, auxin signal was strongly increased in the vascular tissues and auxin reflux in the lateral tissues was absent.
source: Auxin signal was strongly increased in the vascular tissues and auxin reflux in the lateral tissues was absent; again, model predictions closely match experimentally observed patterns (see Figure 1 in Matosevich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results and a citation to published research (Matosevich et al., 2020).

claim: CMTs organization can be modulated by chemical treatments which cause microtubules depolymerization and stimulate the radial expansion of roots.
source: Additionally, we explored whether simulated chemical perturbation of core mechanics would reproduce the experimentally observed root phenotypes. CMTs organization can be modulated by chemical treatments which cause microtubules depolymerization and stimulate the radial expansion of roots (Baskin et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Baskin et al., 1994).

claim: Simulated CMTs disruption by implementing a gradual reduction of the AF during root growth results in marked radial swelling, more evident in the center of the meristem and much less pronounced in the root tip.
source: We simulated CMTs disruption by implementing a gradual reduction of the AF during root growth (Figure 5E and Figure 5—video 7). The simulated root displays a marked radial swelling, more evident in the center of the meristem and much less pronounced in the root tip (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—video 7.

claim: After simulated CMTs disruption, several cells divide irregularly, and the organ loses its anisotropic shape.
source: Several cells divide irregularly, and the organ loses its anisotropic shape.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results.

claim: After simulated CMTs disruption, PINs polarities become more irregular, and asymmetric auxin distribution is eventually lost.
source: As a consequence of this, PINs polarities become more irregular, and asymmetric auxin distribution is eventually lost (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Choosing alternative starting geometries has no visible impact on root anisotropy, auxin distribution, and PIN patterns in the simulations.
source: Also, we tested the model robustness concerning cellular geometry and key model parameters that control PIN polarity and auxin effect on cell growth rates. Choosing alternative staring geometries (Nieuwland et al., 2016; Scheres et al., 1994) has no visible impact on root anisotropy, auxin distribution, and PIN patterns in the simulations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B and citations to published research (Nieuwland et al., 2016; Scheres et al., 1994).

claim: The model predictions are generally robust for a plausible range of parameter values.
source: Similarly, we found our model predictions to be generally robust for a plausible range of parameter values (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: The model can reproduce various root meristem phenotypes including several auxin transport mutants, and mechanical or chemical manipulations of root tissue geometry.
source: These results demonstrate that our model can reproduce various root meristem phenotypes including several auxin transport mutants, and mechanical or chemical manipulations of root tissue geometry.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the model simulation results.

claim: The model could provide a useful tool for guiding wet-lab experimental designs.
source: Thus, our model could provide a useful tool for guiding wet-lab experimental designs.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applications of the model.

claim: Computer models have become a powerful tool for wet-lab scientists to quickly explore possible mechanisms and theories underlying organ growth patterns and thus to guide and design effective experimental strategies.
source: Computer models have become a powerful tool for wet-lab scientists to quickly explore possible mechanisms and theories underlying organ growth patterns and thus to guide and design effective experimental strategies.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the role of computer models in science.

claim: Computer models of root development have been instrumental in understanding root maturation and zonation through biochemical processes integrated over non-growing or idealized templates.
source: To date, computer models of root development have been instrumental in understanding root maturation and zonation through biochemical processes integrated over non-growing (Band et al., 2014; Rutten and Ten Tusscher, 2019) or idealized templates (Grieneisen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Band et al., 2014; Rutten and Ten Tusscher, 2019; Grieneisen et al., 2007).

claim: Little to no attempts were made to couple mechanisms of cell polarity establishment and realistic tissue biomechanics at single-cell resolution to mechanistically understand how root growth and cell polarities are established from small populations of differentiated cells.
source: However, little to no attempts were made to couple mechanisms of cell polarity establishment and realistic tissue biomechanics at single-cell resolution to mechanistically understand how root growth and cell polarities are established from small populations of differentiated cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: The mechanistic cell-based model successfully reproduces important elements of the root meristem morphology including cell polarity organization, auxin distribution, and sustained anisotropic root growth.
source: Here, we took advantage of an efficient modeling technique called Position-Based Dynamics (Müller et al., 2007) to resolve biomechanics of root growth at single-cell resolution, while simultaneously incorporating biochemical reactions that guide auxin production, distribution, and polar transport across tissues. Our mechanistic cell-based model successfully reproduces important elements of the root meristem morphology including cell polarity organization, auxin distribution, and sustained anisotropic root growth.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the model simulation results.

claim: In the model framework, root growth patterns result from local cell growth activities and direct cell-to-cell communication mediated by auxin without the need for global regulators or polarizers.
source: In this framework, root growth patterns result from local cell growth activities and direct cell-to-cell communication mediated by auxin without the need for global regulators or polarizers.
evidence: The claim describes a property of the model.

claim: The model demonstrates that auxin influx from the LRC and subsequent 'bipolar' PINs localization in the cortical tissues may be important elements for sustained auxin-dependent root growth.
source: Furthermore, our model demonstrates that auxin influx from the LRC and subsequent 'bipolar' PINs localization in the cortical tissues may be important elements for sustained auxin-dependent root growth.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: PIN polarity depends on the auxin flow entering the cell but also on mechanical constraints.
source: In particular, we found that PIN polarity depends on the auxin flow entering the cell but also on mechanical constraints, and a plausible molecular mechanism for PIN polarization based on a putative kinase/phosphatase regulation was proposed (Hajný et al., 2020; Michniewicz et al., 2007; Weller et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation results and citations to published research (Hajný et al., 2020; Michniewicz et al., 2007; Weller et al., 2017).

claim: A plausible molecular mechanism for PIN polarization based on a putative kinase/phosphatase regulation was proposed.
source: In particular, we found that PIN polarity depends on the auxin flow entering the cell but also on mechanical constraints, and a plausible molecular mechanism for PIN polarization based on a putative kinase/phosphatase regulation was proposed (Hajný et al., 2020; Michniewicz et al., 2007; Weller et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hajný et al., 2020; Michniewicz et al., 2007; Weller et al., 2017).

claim: The model can be extended to address many aspects of root development and organogenesis including root cells ablation, root response after chemical treatment, and genetic mutations.
source: We further show that our model can be extended to address many aspects of root development and organogenesis including root cells ablation, root response after chemical treatment, and genetic mutations.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the model simulation results.

claim: The quantitative model predictions largely reproduce experimental observations.
source: As the quantitative model predictions largely reproduce experimental observations, our model could be a useful tool to predict the phenotypes of various mutants and test the effects of perturbations such as chemical treatments, gene knockdown, or mechanical alterations, guiding further the effective design of wet-lab experiments.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the model simulation results.

claim: The model could be a useful tool to predict the phenotypes of various mutants and test the effects of perturbations such as chemical treatments, gene knockdown, or mechanical alterations.
source: As the quantitative model predictions largely reproduce experimental observations, our model could be a useful tool to predict the phenotypes of various mutants and test the effects of perturbations such as chemical treatments, gene knockdown, or mechanical alterations, guiding further the effective design of wet-lab experiments.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applications of the model.

claim: In the future, the model could be expanded to address additional mechanisms of root zonation, stem cells differentiation, lateral root initiation, and auxin flux through plasmodesmata.
source: In the future, our model could be expanded to address additional mechanisms of root zonation (Ivanov and Dubrovsky, 2013), stem cells differentiation (Sabatini et al., 2003), lateral root initiation (Perianez-Rodriguez et al., 2021), and auxin flux through plasmodesmata (Mellor et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about future extensions of the model, with citations to published research (Ivanov and Dubrovsky, 2013; Sabatini et al., 2003; Perianez-Rodriguez et al., 2021; Mellor et al., 2020).

claim: The results support the robustness of the model and allow the possibility for modular extensions of the current framework to account for further complexities.
source: These results support the robustness of the model and allow the possibility for modular extensions of the current framework to account for further complexities; for instance, the action of other hormones and postembryonic regulatory mechanisms like gravitropism and phototropism.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model simulation results.

claim: This type of model framework can be employed to model other plant organs at cellular resolution as both auxin and mechanics are important general aspects of organogenesis in plants.
source: Furthermore, this type of model framework can be employed to model other plant organs at cellular resolution as both auxin and mechanics are important general aspects of organogenesis in plants.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applications of the model framework.

claim: The current framework relies on several simplifications and assumptions.
source: Nevertheless, the current framework relies on several simplifications and assumptions; we specified ad-hoc rules for cell division in the stem cell niche patterning, we simplified the combined action of cytoskeleton components such CMTs, actin, and cell wall composition, and chose an initial root tip organization.
evidence: The claim describes limitations of the model.

claim: Future improvements of the current model should focus on the regulation of cell differentiation, auxin-control of stem cell niche maintenance, detailed protein trafficking, tissue-specific expression of auxin transporters, root zonation, and tropism by integrating new experimental insights.
source: Future improvements of the current model should focus on the regulation of cell differentiation, auxin-control of stem cell niche maintenance, detailed protein trafficking, tissue-specific expression of auxin transporters, root zonation, and tropism by integrating new experimental insights.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about future improvements of the model.

claim: An important aspect missing in the current model is rapid cell elongation.
source: An important aspect missing in the current model is rapid cell elongation; this would require the implementation of dynamic tissue remeshing and the preservation of mechano-chemical information.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the model.

claim: The study highlights the general design principles underlying root growth organization determined by local interactions between directional transport of auxin, auxin-dependent cell elongation, cell polarization, and biomechanical stimuli.
source: Taken together, our study highlights the general design principles underlying root growth organization determined by local interactions between directional transport of auxin, auxin-dependent cell elongation, cell polarization, and biomechanical stimuli, and presents a step forward toward quantitative subcellular models of plant organogenesis which could serve as a next-stage platform to develop novel traits of high socio-economic importance.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The study presents a step forward toward quantitative subcellular models of plant organogenesis which could serve as a next-stage platform to develop novel traits of high socio-economic importance.
source: Taken together, our study highlights the general design principles underlying root growth organization determined by local interactions between directional transport of auxin, auxin-dependent cell elongation, cell polarization, and biomechanical stimuli, and presents a step forward toward quantitative subcellular models of plant organogenesis which could serve as a next-stage platform to develop novel traits of high socio-economic importance.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applications of the study.
